1.pericope_label: And as he went out of the temple, one of his disciples saith unto him, Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here! And Jesus answering said unto him, Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.

schools.summary: Ellicott and Robertson both note that Mark alone preserves the disciple's own words, Robertson guessing at Peter and calling the remark a pleasant platitude offered at a crisis; Barnes and Robertson give the stones' dimensions, Barnes from Josephus and Robertson from blocks still standing at the temple angles.
Clarke takes the reported scale of the stones as enough by itself to account for the disciples' wonder.
Henry treats the remark as a symptom of idolizing what looks great, and contrasts Christ's pity for ruined souls with his indifference to a ruined building.
Theophylact answers the objection that ruins were in fact left standing, first by referring the words to the consummation of all things and then by pointing to Hadrian's levelling of city and temple.

Bede sets the widow's mite and the doomed masonry in deliberate sequence and argues the temple had to be removed lest the weak slip back into carnal Judaism; Pseudo-Jerome reads the stones as testimonies of the prophets misapplied to Ezra, Zerubbabel and the Maccabees.

debates.question: Why did the disciple call attention to the buildings?

positions.position: He was idolizing what looks great, pleading that Christ not leave so fine a place
Natural admiration of Galilean peasants still measuring by quantity and size
Perhaps Peter, diverting the Teacher from the grim subjects of the last hours with a commonplace

debates.question: Was the prediction that not one stone would be left literally fulfilled?

positions.position: Yes at the consummation of all things, and in history when Hadrian levelled the city
Yes as far as the building went: the verb means loosened down, and only the foundation stones remain

outliers.claim: Reads the stones as the testimonies of the prophets, none of which would be left standing upon Ezra, Zerubbabel or the Maccabees, to whom the Jews had perversely applied them.

themes: And as he went out of the temple, one of his disciples saith unto him, Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!
And Jesus answering said unto him, Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.

3.pericope_label: And as he sat upon the mount of Olives over against the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, Tell us, when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign when all these things shall be fulfilled?

schools.summary: Barnes and Ellicott place the Mount of Olives and note that Mark alone gives the vantage point, Ellicott adding that it may be the spot where Jesus wept over the city and listing what is peculiar about the four names; Lightfoot recovers the temple practice the phrase over against recalls, the low east wall that let the priest sight the gate while burning the red heifer; Robertson sets out the competing accounts of what this discourse is.
Wesley finds two distinct questions here, one about the destruction of the city and one about the end of the world.
Cyril of Jerusalem takes the apostles' question as a model, warning in both directions at once against declaring the time and against slumbering on that account.
Bede makes the Lord's posture on the mount agree with his words, and Augustine refuses to separate the strands of the answer at all.

debates.question: What is the discourse about?

positions.position: Two distinct questions, the city and the end of the world
Mark's terms are vaguer than the parallel's, perhaps for Gentile readers
Three things at once: the city, the Lord's daily coming through the Church, and the last judgment
One blended picture of his death, the fall of the city, and the second coming it typifies

outliers.claim: Connects over against the temple with the low east wall of the court of the Gentiles, kept low so the priest burning the red heifer on Olivet could sight the temple gate across it.

themes: And as he sat upon the mount of Olives over against the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately,
Tell us, when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign when all these things shall be fulfilled?

5.pericope_label: And Jesus answering them began to say, Take heed lest any man deceive you: For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many. And when ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, be ye not troubled: for such things must needs be; but the end shall not be yet. For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be earthquakes in divers places, and there shall be famines and troubles: these are the beginnings of sorrows.

schools.summary: Robertson brings the warning about deceivers down to the present, observing that in every age men have fitted this picture to the calamity of their own time, and documents the period's wars, famines and earthquakes; Ellicott takes the plain Greek of the impostors' claim to be simply I am He; Lightfoot shows what the phrase about the beginning of sorrows would have stirred in hearers taught to expect Gog and Magog; Barnes supplies the image of a woman in travail behind it.
Clarke reports manuscripts and versions that add the title, making the claim I am the Christ, and notes that many copies have the singular, the beginning.
Henry reads the answer as a redirection from curiosity to conscience and gives four reasons for not being troubled by wars, ending in a holy security of mind while all around is disorder.

Theophylact makes the wars the Romans against the Jews and draws on Josephus for the sequence; Cyril of Jerusalem reckons the prediction of false Christs fulfilled only in part and asks his hearers whether the signs are not already among them.

Bede names the pretenders who appeared while destruction hung over the city and the heresiarchs inside the Church, fixes the interval before the end at some forty years, and alone turns kingdom against kingdom into a figure of heretics.

debates.question: What does kingdom against kingdom describe?

positions.position: The Roman war against the Jews, as Josephus records it
Documented outbreaks, famines and earthquakes between the prophecy and the fall of the city
Heretics fighting one another, whose conflict brings about the triumph of the Church

debates.question: Have the signs already come to pass?

positions.position: Yes, in part and in our own day: Simon and Menander have said it, and there is war now between Persians and Romans
Every age has tried to fit the picture to its own calamity; that is the error the warning guards against

outliers.claim: Quotes a rabbi's rule that when you see the kingdoms disturbing one another you may expect the footsteps of the Messiah, showing what the scribes had taught the nation to look for.

themes: And Jesus answering them began to say, Take heed lest any man deceive you:
For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many.
And when ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, be ye not troubled: for such things must needs be; but the end shall not be yet.
For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be earthquakes in divers places, and there shall be famines and troubles: these are the beginnings of sorrows.

9.pericope_label: But take heed to yourselves: for they shall deliver you up to councils; and in the synagogues ye shall be beaten: and ye shall be brought before rulers and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them. And the gospel must first be published among all nations. But when they shall lead you, and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost. Now the brother shall betray the brother to death, and the father the son; and children shall rise up against their parents, and shall cause them to be put to death. And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the repeated warning is peculiar to Mark and that this block of suffering stands where the parallel discourse lacks it; Robertson identifies the councils with the Jerusalem body and recovers the flaying force of the verb rendered beaten, then fences the promise of the Spirit against lazy preachers; Barnes reads the promise as a pledge of inspiration and argues that for a testimony should be to them rather than against them.

Gill takes the warning to concern the safety of their persons rather than their doctrine; Calvin balances relief from anxiety against indolent security and notes from the parallel that what is promised is the confounding of adversaries, not escape from death.
Clarke sorts the tribunals by rank, from the great Sanhedrin down to the village courts of three magistrates, and identifies the governors and kings.

Theophylact reads for a testimony against them as a judgment given beforehand that leaves the hearers inexcusable, and explains that the apostles' troubles were foretold so they might take comfort in company and prepare for betrayal by their own families.

Bede makes the persecution of the heralds the greatest cause of the nation's ruin and finds the consolation in the greater number gathered from all mankind; the Gloss supplies the fear that the promise of the Spirit answers, that unlearned men would stand speechless before kings.

debates.question: Is the testimony borne against the judges or to them?

positions.position: To them: the disciples stand as witnesses of the truth before their judges
Against them: a judgment given beforehand, leaving them inexcusable

debates.question: How far does the promise of the Spirit reach?

positions.position: To inspiration, so that the recorded defences are the words of the Holy Ghost
To defences before courts only, not to preaching; it excuses no unprepared sermon
To relief from anxiety without indolent security; the promise is that adversaries will be confounded

outliers.claim: Reports that the verse about the gospel going first to all nations is omitted by many lectionaries and thinks its proper place is later in the passage.

themes: But take heed to yourselves: for they shall deliver you up to councils; and in the synagogues ye shall be beaten: and ye shall be brought before rulers and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them.
And the gospel must first be published among all nations.

But when they shall lead you, and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost.
Now the brother shall betray the brother to death, and the father the son; and children shall rise up against their parents, and shall cause them to be put to death.
And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.

14.pericope_label: But when ye shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing where it ought not, (let him that readeth understand,) then let them that be in Judea flee to the mountains: And let him that is on the housetop not go down into the house, neither enter therein, to take any thing out of his house: And let him that is in the field not turn back again for to take up his garment.

schools.summary: Robertson identifies the phrase in the parallel as the one used in the Maccabean history of the altar to Zeus raised by Antiochus, notes that Mark treats the abomination as a person while the third Gospel defines it by the armies, and concludes that the prophet's words find a second fulfilment with Rome in Syria's place.
Gill takes the abomination for the Roman army encircling the city, a thing abominable to the Jews and desolating to nation, city and temple.
Clarke notes only a manuscript expansion of the parenthesis, which he thinks needless; Wesley glosses where it ought not as meaning a place set apart for sacred use.

Henry turns the identification into an exchange, the nation having rejected Christ as an abomination who would have saved them, and presses the affront of heathen standing where they should never have been suffered to come.
Theophylact calls the abomination the violent entry of enemies into the city and observes that the warning names those in Judaea because the apostles were already gone from it.

Bede refuses to settle on one referent, offering Antichrist, Pilate's statue of Caesar and Hadrian's equestrian statue, and reports the Christians' flight to Pella as the prophecy's literal fulfilment; Augustine harmonises Mark's where it ought not with the other reports; the Gloss works through the three hindrances to flight; Pseudo-Jerome turns the flight into an ascent from vice to virtue.

debates.question: What is the abomination of desolation?

positions.position: The Roman army encircling the city
The violent entry of enemies into the city
Antichrist, or Pilate's statue of Caesar, or Hadrian's statue in the holy of holies
The same thing the other accounts describe, fixed by the third as the city compassed with armies

debates.question: Is the flight to the mountains a literal or a moral instruction?

positions.position: Literal, and literally obeyed: the Christians crossed the Jordan and settled at Pella
Literal and urgent; better to be saved naked than delayed by property, children or season
Moral: the ascent to the heights of virtue, not to be exchanged for the depths of sin

outliers.claim: Treats the parenthesis let him that readeth understand as a rule of method, concluding that a saying we are challenged to understand is thereby marked as mystical.

themes: But when ye shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing where it ought not, (let him that readeth understand,) then let them that be in Judea flee to the mountains:
And let him that is on the housetop not go down into the house, neither enter therein, to take any thing out of his house:
And let him that is in the field not turn back again for to take up his garment.

17.pericope_label: But woe to them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days! And pray ye that your flight be not in the winter. For in those days shall be affliction, such as was not from the beginning of the creation which God created unto this time, neither shall be. And except that the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh should be saved: but for the elect’s sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days.

schools.summary: Ellicott points out that Mark omits the clause about the sabbath which is prominent in the parallel, and takes the omission as characteristic of a Gospel for Gentile readers; Robertson notes that the clause naming the elect as those whom he chose stands in Mark alone.
Gill reads the woe to mothers and the prayer about winter practically, and keeps the tribulation to the siege with its zealots, sword, plague and famine.
Wesley alone refuses to close the question, asking whether the affliction has yet been fully accomplished, and identifies the elect as Christians taken out of the world.

Theophylact hears the eating of children in the woe to nursing mothers and explains the shortening as mercy to the Jews who would believe after the city fell; Cyril of Jerusalem sets the tribulation at three years and a half on the prophet's authority and divides his hearers into the stout-hearted who may stand and the fearful who should provide for their safety.

Bede refers the affliction to the times of Antichrist, when miracles will accompany the tormentors, and makes the tribulation shorter in proportion as it is greater; Augustine holds both readings at once by restricting never shall be to that people, and reports a reading in which the days stand for the calamities done in them.

debates.question: Is the great tribulation the Roman war or the reign of Antichrist?

positions.position: The siege and its attendant horrors; the war was cut short for the sake of Jews who would believe
The times of Antichrist, three years and a half, with miracles attending the tormentors
Both, if never shall be is restricted to that people; and the Jews may then be said to cause the later tribulation rather than suffer it
Not yet fully accomplished; much of the affliction may still be to come

debates.question: What does the shortening of the days mean?

positions.position: The war was finished quickly, so that the race was not destroyed
The days stand for the calamities done in them, abridged because God-given patience made them felt less

outliers.claim: Divides his congregation pastorally, telling the stout-hearted to stand because he does not despair of the Church's nerve and the fearful to provide for their own safety.

themes: But woe to them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days!
And pray ye that your flight be not in the winter.
For in those days shall be affliction, such as was not from the beginning of the creation which God created unto this time, neither shall be.
And except that the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh should be saved: but for the elect’s sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days.

21.pericope_label: And then if any man shall say to you, Lo, here is Christ; or, lo, he is there; believe him not: For false Christs and false prophets shall rise, and shall shew signs and wonders, to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect. But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things.

schools.summary: Robertson notes that Mark's construction expresses purpose where the parallel expresses result, and answers the warning in his own voice, that gullibility is no mark of piety and credulity ranks no higher than scepticism; Ellicott observes that the repeated warning word is again peculiar to Mark.
Gill records that false Christs arose both before and after the destruction of the city, and holds together the certainty of the elect's salvation with the duty of using every means of perseverance.
Theophylact denies that then means immediately after the fall of Jerusalem, citing the indefinite use of the same word elsewhere, and refers the warning to the time of Antichrist.

Bede rejects the application to the Jewish war on the ground that no Christian was in the city to be warned, preferring heretics from Simon Magus to Antichrist; Augustine leaves open whether the lying wonders are illusions or true marvels that mislead; Gregory turns the conditional if it were possible into a definition of election.

debates.question: To what period does the warning about false Christs belong?

positions.position: Both before and after the destruction of the city
The time of Antichrist; then is used indefinitely, not as a sequence
Heretics opposing the Church, from Simon Magus to Antichrist; no Christian was in the besieged city to be warned

debates.question: In what sense are Antichrist's wonders lying?

positions.position: Either they deceive the senses with phantoms or they are real and mislead men ignorant of Satan's power; either way those deceived deserve it

outliers.claim: Turns if it were possible into a definition: if they are elect it is not possible, and if it is possible they are not elect; the hesitation expresses the trembling of the elect, not the Lord's uncertainty.

themes: And then if any man shall say to you, Lo, here is Christ; or, lo, he is there; believe him not:
For false Christs and false prophets shall rise, and shall shew signs and wonders, to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect.
But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things.

24.pericope_label: But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, And the stars of heaven shall fall, and the powers that are in heaven shall be shaken. And then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven.

schools.summary: Robertson warns that the darkened lights are prophetic imagery not meant to be taken literally, citing Peter's use of the same prophecy at Pentecost, and notes that the phrase from the tip of earth to the tip of heaven occurs nowhere else; Ellicott observes that Mark's plain they shall see the Son of man replaces the parallel's sign of the Son of man, and that the trumpet is absent here.

Gill reads the whole passage of the first century: the falling stars are the rabbins who set the oral law above scripture, the seeing is the power of Christ's wrath, and the angels sent out are gospel ministers planting churches among the Gentiles.
Wesley takes the days as those immediately preceding the end of the world.

Henry makes the phrase after that tribulation the correction of the disciples' confusion of the city's fall with the end, and warns against concluding that because the Son of man did not visibly come then he never would.

Theophylact reads the falling stars as the angelic powers astonished at the judging of their fellow-servants, argues from the visible body that what is seen is body, and takes Christ's sending of the angels as proof of his equality with the Father; Cyril of Jerusalem makes the sign of the coming a luminous Cross going before the King.

Bede explains the darkening as the lights being outshone by the true Light while allowing a real loss of light as at the Passion, and guards the gathering against the idea that only the world's edges are searched; Augustine argues from the manner of the Ascension that the Lord comes in the same body and on a cloud, and that the Son of man received power to judge because the wicked cannot see the form of God; Pseudo-Jerome reads every celestial term morally.

debates.question: Do these verses describe the fall of Jerusalem or the end of the world?

positions.position: The end: after that tribulation separates the two, and the disciples had confounded them
The first century throughout: the rabbis are the stars, the wrath is the seeing, the gospel ministers are the angels

debates.question: Are the sun, moon and stars literally darkened?

positions.position: The imagery is prophetic and apocalyptic, not to be pressed literally
They are outshone by the brightness of the true Light, though a real loss of light is not excluded
Morally: the sun darkened at the coldness of hearts, the stars failing as the seed of Abraham disappears

outliers.claim: Argues from the sending of the angels that Christ despatches them as the Father does, and asks where then are they who say he is not equal to the Father.

themes: But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light,
And the stars of heaven shall fall, and the powers that are in heaven shall be shaken.
And then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory.
And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven.

28.pericope_label: Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When her branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is near: So ye in like manner, when ye shall see these things come to pass, know that it is nigh, even at the doors. Verily I say unto you, that this generation shall not pass, till all these things be done. Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away.

schools.summary: Ellicott raises a textual point that reaches past the verse, taking the reading it is known for an early copyist's slip in the document he supposes underlies all three reports.

Gill places the parable on the Mount of Olives in the season for figs, takes this generation strictly of the men then living, and allows the passing of heaven and earth either as statement or as comparison.

Clarke argues for a second sense of the word, this very race of men, conceding that it can mean a term of thirty-eight years, which is exactly the interval to the destruction, but preferring the other because events in the chapter look beyond it; Wesley narrows what is promised instead, taking all these things of the temple and the city.
Henry notes that the disciples themselves were taken from the evil to come, all but one, while the generation they trained up lived to see it.

Theophylact reads the parable for its speed, summer following leaves as the coming of Christ follows the woes of Antichrist, excludes the apostles from this generation and makes it the generation of Christians, and takes the elements as failing before Christ's words do.

Bede makes the fig tree the synagogue, barren now but yielding its withheld fruit when the fulness of the Gentiles is come in, leaves this generation open between mankind and the Jews, and restricts the passing heaven to the region of the air; Augustine refers nearly the whole discourse to the Lord's daily coming in his body the Church.

debates.question: What does this generation mean?

positions.position: The men then living, and no wider
This very race of men, since events in the chapter look beyond the destruction
The generation of Christians; most of the apostles did not live to see the city fall
Either the whole race of mankind or the Jews in particular
The question is settled by narrowing all these things to the temple and the city

outliers.claim: Treats a variant here as a slip in a common written source behind all three Gospels, which then stopped and left the evangelists to their own memories.

themes: Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When her branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is near:
So ye in like manner, when ye shall see these things come to pass, know that it is nigh, even at the doors.
Verily I say unto you, that this generation shall not pass, till all these things be done.
Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away.

32.pericope_label: But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father. Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is.

schools.summary: Robertson holds that the disclaimer of knowledge applies to the second coming, the fall of the city having just been fixed within that generation, and is certain the clause is genuine here; Barnes defends its genuineness, dismisses the evasion that the verb means to make known, and rests on the finite knowledge of a real human nature; Ellicott notes the characteristic repetition of the warning word and suggests the three Gospels rested on a common document that stopped at this point.
Gill refers the day and hour to Jerusalem's destruction, since Christ had been speaking of nothing else, and makes the concealment the reason for the command to watch.

Clarke finds the ignorance unaccountable, suspects on the evidence of the parallels that the clause was not original, and can explain it only by supposing the indwelling Deity communicated less knowledge at one time than another; Wesley notes that that day is scripture's emphatic name for the judgment.
Theophylact points out that the words say ye know not rather than I do not know, and treats the concealment as mercy, since men careless in ignorance would be worse if they knew the end.
Hilary refuses the inference from ignorance altogether, and resolves the saying by the hiding of the treasures of wisdom that are in Christ.

debates.question: Which day and hour are unknown?

positions.position: Jerusalem's destruction, of which alone Christ had been speaking
The second coming; the city's fall had just been fixed within that generation

debates.question: In what sense does the Son not know?

positions.position: The clause may not be original; if it is, the indwelling Deity communicated less knowledge at that moment
As man his knowledge was finite, as it was when he increased in wisdom and stature
Not ignorance at all: the treasures of wisdom are in him but hidden, and the saying reports the hiding
The text says ye know not, and the concealment was mercy toward the careless

outliers.claim: Argues that to make the Father withhold this knowledge ascribes envy to him, since he gave the Son foreknowledge of his own death.

themes: But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father.
Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is.

34.pericope_label: For the Son of man is as a man taking a far journey, who left his house, and gave authority to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch. Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning: Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.

schools.summary: Barnes and Robertson identify the four watches into which the night was reckoned and read the porter as the door-keeper charged with the house; Ellicott fixes the hours, notes that the words making the opening sentence work are absent from the Greek, and proposes that this is a fragmentary report of material developed elsewhere as the parables of the talents and of the virgins.
Gill notes that the discourse was given privately to the four who had asked.
Clarke makes the porter the ministers of the gospel, who should watch continually for the whole flock, and asks whether a prisoner expecting deliverance needs to be told to be ready.
Theophylact turns the four watches into the span of one life, evening being death in old age and cockcrow the age when reason comes to its strength.

Bede identifies the traveller as Christ ascending after the Resurrection, withdrawing his bodily but not his divine presence; Gregory locates the far country in the heavens where the flesh was set and widens the porter's office from pastors to every heart; Augustine argues that since the last day will not find all men living, the command reaches each man at his own death; Pseudo-Jerome compares the worldly to sleepers who wake possessing nothing of what they saw.

debates.question: Who is the porter commanded to watch?

positions.position: The literal door-keeper entrusted with the house
The ministers of the gospel, watching for the safety of the flock
The order of pastors, but also every one of us at the door of his own heart
A feature unique among the parables, whose special interpretation is genuinely open

debates.question: Is the coming to be watched for the last day or one's own death?

positions.position: Each man's own end, since that day will not find all men living
A promise deliberately left undefined as to times and seasons, each watch answering to centuries of history

outliers.claim: Points to the Christian names meaning watchful, Gregory and Vigilius among them, as evidence of how deeply this command took hold.

themes: For the Son of man is as a man taking a far journey, who left his house, and gave authority to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch.
Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning:
Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping.
And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
